items.title: 30% transport fare hike still on the table, talks resume Tuesday – GPRTU
items.description: The Ghana Private Road Transport Union (GPRTU) has rejected claims by the National Petroleum Authority (NPA) that its proposed 30% increase in transport fares has been put on hold. The union says no agreement has been reached with government to suspend the proposed adjustment, insisting that negotiations with the Ministry of Transport remain inconclusive. Speaking on Joynews, deputy Public Relations Officer of the GPRTU, Samuel Amoah, said the two sides were still negotiating the proposed increase at their last meeting on Friday, September 18. “There has never been any agreement with the government that we are suspending our proposed increment. The last meeting we had with the minister was last Friday, and we were still negotiating the 30 percent increase, but there wasn’t any conclusion,” he said. His comments contradict an earlier position by NPA Chief Executive, Godwin Edudzi Tamakloe, who said engagements with transport operators had helped put the planned fare increase “on ice.” Mr Tamakloe said government and transport operators had been discussing how to manage the impact of rising fuel prices and other operating costs without immediately passing the full burden on to commuters. Mr Amoah said the GPRTU remains committed to its proposed 30% adjustment, although the union is prepared to negotiate. He said the union had indicated during Friday’s meeting that any reduction from the proposed 30% would not take the figure below 25%. “We are pushing for 30% increment. That is what was on the table at the last Friday negotiation. And we made the ministry understand that if we have to come down, we still come anything less than 25%. And that is where we ended it,” he said. The GPRTU had earlier submitted a proposal for a fare review to the Ministry of Transport, with a joint team comprising the ministry, the GPRTU and the Ghana Road Transport Coordinating Council (GRTCC) tasked with reviewing the various cost inputs before a final decision is taken. The union had also previously stated that existing approved fares remained in force while the review process was ongoing. Mr Amoah cited rising fuel prices, spare parts, insurance and vehicle maintenance among the factors behind the proposed adjustment. The development comes after the NPA raised the price floor for petrol and diesel from September 16, with the authority setting the floors at GH¢16 per litre for petrol and GH¢16.77 for diesel. Some Oil Marketing Companies subsequently adjusted their pump prices. The GPRTU has argued that the higher fuel costs have compounded existing pressures from other inputs required to operate commercial vehicles. According to Mr Amoah, the GPRTU and the Ministry of Transport are expected to resume discussions on Tuesday, September 22. He said the parties had agreed to postpone their meeting because Monday, September 21, was a public holiday. “We all agreed that tomorrow morning we’ll go back to the transport ministry again to conclude the percentage increment,” he said. The outcome of that engagement will determine whether the proposed adjustment is maintained, reduced or otherwise revised. Meanwhile, Mr Amoah said GPRTU members have been directed not to participate in a sit-down strike announced by the Progressive Transport Owners Association (PROTOA) over the rising cost of vehicle maintenance. The directive comes amid broader concerns among commercial transport operators about the cost of keeping vehicles on the road. For now, however, the GPRTU’s proposed fare adjustment remains subject to negotiations with government, with no new fare officially approved.

items.title: Dr Khadim Niang : « Les Houthis bénéficient d’une géographie extrêmement favorable »
items.description: Titulaire d’un doctorat en Sciences politiques avec une thèse portant sur la « Géopolitique des ressources et défis sécuritaires en Afrique : le cas du golfe de Guinée », Dr Khadim Niang est également ingénieur en génie civil diplômé de l’École polytechnique de Thiès (Ept). Dans cet entretien, il revient sur la nouvelle donne imposée par les Houthis dans le paysage sécuritaire du Moyen-Orient. Comment un mouvement armé comme celui des Houthis, longtemps considéré comme un acteur périphérique du Moyen-Orient, est-il aujourd’hui en mesure de faire peser une menace aussi sérieuse sur l’une des régions les plus stratégiques du monde ? Pour comprendre la puissance actuelle des Houthis, il faut d’abord regarder une carte. C’est, à mon avis, le meilleur moyen d’appréhender la géopolitique. Les Houthis ne sont pas devenus subitement une superpuissance militaire ; ils bénéficient avant tout d’une géographie extrêmement favorable. Le Yémen borde la mer Rouge et se situe à proximité immédiate du détroit de Bab el-Mandeb, passage stratégique reliant l’océan Indien, la mer Rouge et le canal de Suez. Lorsqu’un acteur disposant de missiles, de drones et de capacités navales se trouve au niveau d’un tel point d’étranglement, son poids stratégique devient beaucoup plus important que sa puissance économique ou militaire réelle. À cela s’ajoute leur expérience du combat. Les Houthis ont résisté pendant plusieurs années à une coalition dirigée par l’Arabie saoudite et ont progressivement développé des capacités de frappe à longue distance. Ils bénéficient également du soutien de l’Iran, même s’il faut éviter de les réduire à un simple instrument de Téhéran. Ils disposent, en effet, de leur propre agenda politique et militaire au Yémen. Les développements récents ont encore changé la donne avec leur progression spectaculaire sur la façade occidentale du Yémen. Celle-ci leur a permis de prendre des positions stratégiques autour de Bab el-Mandeb, notamment à Mokha et sur l’île de Perim, au cœur même du détroit. C’est là tout le paradoxe : un acteur n’a pas nécessairement besoin d’être une grande puissance pour exercer une influence majeure. Il lui suffit parfois de contrôler ou simplement d’être en mesure de menacer le bon territoire au bon moment. Après le détroit d'Ormuz, celui de Bab el-Mandeb se trouve lui aussi menacé de blocage. Quels impacts cela peut-il avoir sur le marché énergétique mondial ? Il faut comprendre que le système énergétique mondial dépend de quelques passages maritimes très étroits. Ormuz en est un, Bab el-Mandeb en est un autre. C’est justement la combinaison des risques sur ces deux zones qui rend la situation particulièrement préoccupante. L’Arabie saoudite dispose certes d’une solution permettant de contourner Ormuz : l’oléoduc Est-Ouest, qui transporte le pétrole depuis l'est du pays jusqu’à Yanbu, sur la mer Rouge. Mais, une fois arrivé à Yanbu, ce pétrole doit encore emprunter les routes maritimes de la mer Rouge. Or, cette voie alternative se trouve elle-même fragilisée par la menace houthie et par les attaques visant les infrastructures énergétiques saoudiennes. Si le passage par Bab el-Mandeb devient trop dangereux, il existe une autre option : contourner toute l’Afrique par le cap de Bonne-Espérance. Voyons ce que cela implique concrètement : une traversée pétrolière classique entre le golfe Persique et le nord-ouest de l’Europe prend environ 19 jours via Suez, contre près de 35 jours en passant par le cap de Bonne-Espérance. On parle donc d'une hausse de la consommation de carburant, de navires immobilisés plus longtemps, de primes d’assurance plus élevées et, au final, d’une augmentation globale des coûts du transport maritime. L’Arabie saoudite, grande puissance régionale, ne parvient toujours pas à neutraliser la menace houthie. Cette organisation peut-elle réellement tenir tête à l’État saoudien ? Il faut distinguer deux notions : la puissance conventionnelle et la capacité de nuisance stratégique. Sur le papier, il n’y a évidemment pas de comparaison possible entre les moyens financiers ou militaires de l’Arabie saoudite et ceux des Houthis. Mais, les conflits contemporains nous enseignent qu’une supériorité militaire écrasante ne garantit pas la victoire face à un acteur asymétrique bien implanté sur son territoire. L’Arabie saoudite en a fait l’expérience durant les années de guerre au Yémen. Les Houthis ont survécu aux bombardements, conservé Sanaa et développé leurs capacités en matière de drones et de missiles. Les événements récents démontrent que leur capacité de nuisance demeure intacte : progression territoriale, attaques d'infrastructures énergétiques et frappes revendiquées sur le sol saoudien. Il faut désormais intégrer une nouvelle variable : l’Alliance de La Mecque entre l’Arabie saoudite, la Turquie et le Pakistan. Cet accord de défense prévoit particulièrement qu’une attaque contre l’un des membres soit considérée comme une attaque contre les autres. La Turquie vient d’ailleurs d’indiquer qu’elle pourrait contribuer à répondre à certains besoins militaires saoudiens. Cette crise pourrait donc constituer un test majeur pour cette nouvelle architecture de sécurité. La véritable question n’est donc pas de savoir si les Houthis peuvent « vaincre » militairement l’Arabie saoudite, mais s’ils réussissent à lui imposer un coût sécuritaire, économique et politique suffisamment élevé pour faire fléchir ses choix. C’est l'essence même d'une stratégie asymétrique et les Houthis font la démonstration de cette capacité aujourd’hui. Entretien réalisé par Oumar NDIAYE

items.title: Éliminatoires CAN 2027: les 48 affiches des deux premières journées dévoilées
items.description: Du 24 septembre au 6 octobre 2026, les sélections africaines disputeront les deux premières journées des éliminatoires de la CAN 2027. Au total, 48 rencontres sont au programme, avec des affiches très attendues. La course à la qualification s’ouvre avec une première série de rencontres réparties sur plusieurs jours, avant la suite du calendrier jusqu’au 6 octobre. Tous les horaires sont indiqués en temps universel (TU). Première journée Jeudi 24 septembre À 13h: Namibie-Congo-Brazzaville (Groupe G). À 16h: Mauritanie-Centrafrique (F), RD Congo-Guinée équatoriale (E), Libye- Botswana (H). À 19h: Côte d’Ivoire-Ghana, Sierra Leone-Zimbabwe (E), Cameroun-Comores (G) et Tunisie -Ouganda (H). Vendredi 25 septembre À 13h: Sénégal-Mozambique (J) et Tanzanie-Guinée-Bissau (L). À 15h: Niger-Lesotho (A). À 16h: Malawi-Soudan du Sud (B), Gambie-Somalie (C), Togo-Burundi (I), Soudan-Éthiopie (J), Rwanda-Liberia (K) et Nigeria-Madagascar (L). À 19h: Maroc-Gabon (A), Égypte-Angola (B), Burkina Faso-Bénin (F), Algérie-Zambie (I) et Mali-Cap-Vert (K). Samedi 26 septembre À 13h: Kenya-Érythrée (D). À 16h: Afrique du Sud-Guinée (D). Deuxième journée Lundi 28 septembre À 16h: Guinée équatoriale-Sierra Leone (E), Zimbabwe-RD Congo (E) et Centrafrique-Burkina Faso (F). À 19h: Botswana-Tunisie (H). Mardi 29 septembre À 11h: Comores-Namibie (G). À 13h: Lesotho-Maroc (A), Soudan du Sud-Égypte (B), Burundi-Algérie (I), Mozambique-Soudan (J), Éthiopie-Sénégal (J) et Madagascar-Tanzanie (L). À 16h: Zambie-Togo (I), Ghana-Gambie (C), Ouganda -Libye (H), Guinée-Bissau-Nigeria (L) et Cap-Vert-Rwanda (K). À 19h: Gabon-Niger (A), Somalie-Côte d’Ivoire (C), Bénin-Mauritanie (F), Congo-Brazzaville -Cameroun (G) et Liberia-Mali (K). Mercredi 30 septembre À 16h: Érythrée-Afrique du Sud (D). Jeudi 1er octobre À 16h: Guinée – Kenya (D). Mardi 6 octobre À 19h: Angola – Malawi (B). Ces premières rencontres lanceront la lutte pour les places qualificatives à la phase finale de la CAN 2027, prévue du 19 juin au 18 juillet 2027 au Kenya, en Ouganda et en Tanzanie. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Éliminatoires CAN 2027: les 48 affiches des deux premières journées dévoilées est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Trophée des Champions : King Vert couronné, la Fondation Fabrice Simporé Global Initiatives fait du sport un levier d’unité
items.description: Après une finale haletante face à Waguess, l'équipe de King Vert a remporté la troisième édition du Trophée des Champions au terme d'une séance de tirs au but (4-2), le dimanche 20 septembre 2026 au Stade municipal de Ziniaré. Un sacre qui vient couronner une initiative portée par la Fondation Fabrice Simporé Global Initiatives (FSGI), placée cette année sous le signe de la discipline, de l'unité et de l'engagement patriotique. Le Stade municipal de Ziniaré a vibré jusqu'au bout. La grande finale de la troisième édition du Trophée des Champions a tenu toutes ses promesses. Après avoir perdu la finale à la 2e édition, King Vert remporte la 3e édition du Trophée des champions Opposée à l'équipe de Waguess, la formation de King Vert, finaliste malheureuse lors de la deuxième édition, a pris sa revanche au terme d'une rencontre longtemps indécise. À l'issue des soixante minutes de temps réglementaire, les deux équipes n'avaient pu se départager, le tableau d'affichage affichant un score nul et vierge de 0-0. C'est finalement dans l'épreuve des tirs au but que King Vert a fait la différence, s'imposant 4 tirs à 2 et soulevant enfin le trophée tant convoité. Cette troisième édition, placée sous le thème : « La discipline du sport en faveur de l'unité et de l'engagement patriotique », s'inscrit dans le programme « Jeunesse, Paix et Sécurité » porté par la Fondation Fabrice Simporé Global Initiatives (FSGI) dans la Région de Oubri. Le General de division Célestin Simporé, ministre d'État, patron de la 3e édition Un cadre qui dépasse largement le seul enjeu sportif. « Au-delà du football, cette finale est surtout un moment de rassemblement pour notre région. Depuis sa création, le Trophée des Champions porte une conviction simple : le sport peut être un puissant instrument de discipline, de paix, de cohésion sociale, d’unité et d’engagement patriotique », a rappelé le promoteur de l'initiative, Fabrice Simporé, président de la FSGI. Interrogé sur la signification du thème de cette édition, le promoteur insiste sur la portée éducative de la compétition. « Sur le terrain, nous apprenons à respecter les règles, à travailler en équipe, à accepter l’autre, à reconnaître le mérite et à rester dignes dans la victoire comme dans la défaite. Ce sont ces mêmes valeurs que nous voulons voir grandir dans notre société. À travers le Programme Jeunesse, Paix et Sécurité, la Fondation Fabrice Simporé Global Initiatives entend contribuer, avec notre jeunesse, à la construction et à la préservation de la paix, en créant des espaces de rencontre, de dialogue et de fraternité », a-t-il souligné. Fabrice Simporé, président de la FSGI, promoteur du Trophée des champions La troisième édition a bénéficié du patronage du Général de Division Célestin Simporé, Ministre d'État, Ministre de la Guerre et de la Défense Patriotique, dont l'accompagnement s'inscrit dans la continuité de celui apporté à l'édition précédente. Édouard Bonkoungou, Président du COGEF de la Région de Oubri, a pour sa part assuré le parrainage de cette édition. « Son soutien multiforme et son accompagnement ont été déterminants dans la tenue de l'activité », salue le promoteur. La troisième édition a également pu compter sur l'engagement du secteur privé, avec I-FRONTLINE comme sponsor officiel, un groupe burkinabè actif notamment dans les infrastructures, les technologies, les systèmes de sécurité et les télécommunications. Un partenariat qui illustre, selon les organisateurs, la volonté de mobiliser les entreprises nationales autour des initiatives destinées à la jeunesse et à la cohésion sociale. Le jeu entre les deux finalistes sous le regard attentif du public Dans les tribunes, l'engouement était palpable. « C'est plus qu'un match de football. On sent que tout le monde est rassemblé, les jeunes, les anciens, les autorités. C'est ça qui est beau », témoigne Ibrahim Sawadogo, supporter venu soutenir l'équipe de King Vert. Pour Awa Ouédraogo, une autre spectatrice, l'initiative mérite d'être saluée : « Le Trophée donne une chance aux jeunes de la région de montrer leur talent. Et le message de discipline et d'unité qu'on nous répète ici, c'est important pour notre pays », a-t-elle souligné. Lancée avec seize équipes lors de la première édition, la compétition est passée à vingt formations lors de la deuxième édition, organisée du 28 juin au 21 septembre 2025 au Stade municipal de Ziniaré. Cette année-là, Sagesse FC avait dominé King Vert en finale sur le score de deux buts à zéro. Trois ans après ses débuts, l'initiative entend désormais franchir un nouveau cap. « Le Trophée des Champions, est notre affaire à tous ! Le Trophée des Champions est aujourd’hui un événement régional à vocation nationale. Né ici, il doit grandir avec notre région et devenir progressivement une vitrine de l’excellence de nos trois provinces et de nos communes. Il ne doit pas rester l’affaire de ses promoteurs ou de son comité d’organisation. Il doit devenir notre affaire à tous. Il appartient à nos jeunes, à nos sportifs, à nos autorités, à nos collectivités, à nos coutumiers et religieux, à nos associations, à nos acteurs économiques, à nos artistes, à nos enseignants, à nos cadres, à nos médias et à toutes les forces vives de notre territoire. Approprions-nous le Trophée des Champions. Faisons-en un espace de rencontre, de fraternité, de valorisation des talents et de cohésion entre nos territoires », ambitionne Fabrice Simporé. Une réflexion est d'ailleurs engagée sur l'évolution de la structuration, de la forme, du contenu et de la périodicité de la compétition, en concertation avec les forces vives et les partenaires. Le finaliste malheureux recevant ses lots La remise du trophée et des distinctions, sous les applaudissements d'un public nombreux, a refermé une saison placée sous le signe de la fraternité et de l'engagement citoyen. King Vert est reparti avec le trophée, un jeu de maillot, des médailles et un enveloppe financière de 500 000 FCFA. Le finaliste malheureux est reparti avec des médailles, un jeu de maillot, un ballon et une enveloppe financière de 300 000 FCFA. À noter que l'équipe classée 3e et 4e, le meilleur gardien, le meilleur buteur et joueur ont tous été primés. items.title: El PP mantiene el pulso por Ceuta: Feijóo y Vivas rechazan los traslados de los menores y acusan al Gobierno de querer una crisis “cronificada”
items.description: No hay cambio de guion, el Partido Popular mantiene el pulso con el Gobierno por Ceuta y se reafirma en rechazar los traslados de menores migrantes a la Península . El presidente de Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, ha ratificado este lunes su negativa al traslado de los menores, de los que su Gobierno ostenta la tutela, y ha instado al Ejecutivo central a “activar los mecanismos necesarios” para devolverlos a Marruecos. Vivas se ha manifestado así en presencia del líder del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, que ha viajado este lunes a Ceuta por cuarta vez desde la entrada masiva de migrantes de finales de julio, acompañado del líder del PP europeo, Manfred Weber, y en la ciudad autónoma ha insistido también en que la única vía que contempla su partido es la expulsión de todos los migrantes que entraron de forma irregular. Feijóo y Vivas han lanzado, además, un nuevo ataque contra el Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez, al que acusan de pretender que la crisis ceutí se “cronifique” de forma deliberada. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Interior Minister Naqvi warns PTI against Sept 27 protest call, urges party to change course
items.description: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Monday warned PTI against its proposed September 27 long march, urging the party to refrain from proceeding with the protest. Naqvi’s remarks come as the party prepares for a nationwide protest and march towards Islamabad on September 27 to press for the release of its incarcerated founder, Imran Khan. “We have clearly told them (PTI) that they can never achieve anything through such drama, and I will say again that there is still time; they should not go into this situation,” Naqvi said during a press briefing, advising the party to “not enter a dead-end street”. The interior minister vowed the government will not “leave any loopholes” in its response if the party went ahead with the protest. He held that PTI’s majority leadership was not in favour of the march. “[However], if they do, then we have the Islamabad High Court (IHC) order , and the government will ensure its implementation.” The IHC order, issued on September 14, ruled that no political party or its leadership has the “lawful right to occupy public roads, highways, interchanges, toll plazas and buildings in Islamabad”. Naqvi appealed to PTI to adopt a different approach. “Do not harm yourself and your workers,” he said. On being asked if the government had any “long-term solution” to PTI’s frequent protest calls, the interior minister said, “I believe this time we will find a permanent solution; we will not leave it halfway.” When asked why the government was reluctant to shift PTI founder Imran Khan to a private health facility — as requested by his party and family — amid concerns about his health, the minister said doctors examined Imran last night. “If they demand that his check-up should be done at a hospital, then we did have one last night [..] we are already fulfilling the demand,” Naqvi said. “As for the treatment that is prescribed under the law, we will do everything according to the law. But we will not do it simply because they are demanding it,” the interior minister added. Naqvi, during his talk, reiterated that PTI’s senior leadership was not in favour of the march. On being asked if the interior ministry will fulfil its role in the upcoming protests, he said, “This time, we will fulfil our role completely. As I said, it will be once and for all.” When asked whether the federal government had any plans to ban the party, the interior minister reiterated, “As I am telling you, this time we will find a once-and-for-all solution. We cannot afford this every time.” Naqvi was also asked if the government was considering imposing governor rule in PTI-led Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP). At this, the minister said, “Look, we have already made it clear to them that whatever legal options are available, the prime minister, in consultation with our law ministry, will utilise them.” However, he clarified that the party will not be allowed to “come to Islamabad and shut down the city for ten days. That possibility does not exist”. Naqvi also spoke about the creation of new provinces, saying that the matter was progressing rapidly and that public participation in the campaign had increased. He said: “The new provinces issue is moving forward at a pace that we cannot even imagine. The way people are practically coming forward, whether they are chambers, traders or individuals, everyone is playing their role in one way or another. I am very hopeful that, God willing, and if the public wants it, new provinces will certainly be created. “And as far as the movement for new provinces is concerned, I believe it is moving ahead rapidly,” he added. Naqvi’s warning comes as part of the government’s pushback against the party’s proposed march. Last week, following the IHC judgement , Naqvi warned that the government would stop anyone from marching towards the federal capital “in every possible way”. ‘No violent group will be allowed’ Speaking to media in Kohat later in the day, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar reiterated that no “violent group will be allowed to descend upon Islamabad”. “I cannot remember a peaceful PTI protest in the recent past,” Tarar said. “Though I absolutely remember that Rangers and police personnel were martyred. Peaceful protesters do not leave their homes armed with sticks, nails, glass or slingshots,” he added. The information minister accused the party’s demonstrators of damaging state property and harassing women, recalling that they had allegedly set a Metro station and trees on fire during one of their demonstrations in Islamabad. “They should never even use the word ‘peaceful’ since they have never been peaceful nor can remain so. Therefore, no violent group can be allowed to enter Islamabad,” he declared. Tarar also accused the PTI government of corruption and “bad intentions” in KP, questioning where the law and order funding was being spent in the wake of last week’s deadly Kohat blast . He slammed KP Chief Minister Sohail Afridi for going to Lahore and “recording videos on a charpoi” — a trip that concluded days before the Kohat blast — rather than staying in his province. “Who will answer for the additional NFC (National Finance Commission Award) funds that have exceeded Rs150 billion?” Tarar asked, alleging that the funds were being used for political purposes. “You have to answer for where you spent the law and order fund as policemen are sacrificing their lives,” he added, addressing Afridi and noting that the money should have been invested in police training and technical enhancement. Tarar had also expressed the government’s determination not to allow any violent group to enter Islamabad or block roads on Sunday, stressing that the administration would ensure compliance with an IHC order against disruption to public movement. Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb on Sunday also warned that strikes, sit-ins, long marches and road closures could cause an estimated Rs120 billion loss to the economy each day.

items.title: Sénégal : 3,2 milliards FCFA de transferts monétaires pour 16 037 ménages agricoles
items.description: Le Programme de Résilience Agricole (PRA) est entré dans sa phase de distribution. Selon un communiqué de presse, la ministre de la Famille, de l'Action sociale et des Solidarités, Marie Angélique Mame Selbé Diouf, a présidé dimanche 20 septembre le lancement officiel des transferts monétaires. Le programme vise à « faciliter l'accès aux intrants essentiels » pour les ménages d'agriculteurs, d'éleveurs et de pêcheurs inscrits au Registre National Unique (RNU), précise le ministère. Pour cette édition 2026, 16 037 ménages agrosylvopastoraux et halieutiques bénéficient du dispositif. Ils viennent des départements de Foundiougne, Guinguinéo, Kaffrine et Ziguinchor. Chaque ménage recevra « une allocation directe de 200 000 FCFA », soit un investissement global de 3 207 400 000 FCFA. Ce total correspond bien au produit du nombre de ménages par le montant unitaire. Deux bénéficiaires ont reçu leur transfert lors de l'événement : Aminata Sarr, transformatrice de produits halieutiques à Foundiougne, et Mamadou Fané, agriculteur dans la commune de Saloum Diané. Le ministère dénonce des « montages vidéo mensongers » Le communiqué consacre une partie à la polémique numérique. Le ministère « constate avec regret » que des contenus visuels de la cérémonie font l'objet de manipulations sur les réseaux sociaux, « à travers des montages vidéo mensongers et des commentaires biaisés ». Il invite les citoyens à la vigilance et « réserve son droit de donner suite » à ces actes de désinformation. Le ministère rappelle que le programme s'inscrit dans la vision du président Bassirou Diomaye Diakhar Faye, définie dans l'Agenda national de Transformation « Sénégal 2050 ». Cet agenda vise, selon lui, à bâtir « une souveraineté alimentaire durable » autour de l'agriculture, de la pêche et de l'élevage. O.B.N

items.title: KATH marks 70th anniversary with inter-directorate games
items.description: The Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital (KATH) has marked its 70th anniversary with an inter-directorate fun games event aimed at strengthening staff bonds, promoting teamwork and encouraging healthy lifestyles among employees. The event, held at Paa Joe Stadium, KNUST, brought together staff from various directorates, members of management and families for a day of sporting and recreational activities. The programme featured football, athletics, table tennis, volleyball, basketball and indoor games, providing staff with an opportunity to interact outside their usual work environments. Speaking at the event, Dr. Yaw Opare Larbi, Deputy Medical Director and Chairman of the KATH 70th Anniversary Operational Committee, said the games were organised to bring staff together and foster stronger relationships across the hospital. “Activities such as this bring us together and we get to make new friends. And this is important for teamwork. It’s important for cohesion,” he said. He said the event was particularly significant because it formed part of the hospital’s celebrations to mark seven decades of service. According to Dr. Larbi, KATH has more than 6,000 staff, making activities that encourage interaction important to building unity and improving teamwork. He also said the games had a health-promotion component, giving staff an opportunity to exercise while encouraging them to become more conscious of their physical wellbeing. Anniversary activities Dr. Larbi said KATH’s 70th anniversary celebrations were launched in December 2025, following the hospital’s attainment of 70 years in 2025, with activities scheduled throughout the anniversary year. One of the activities already undertaken was an outreach in Nkoranza in the Bono East Region, where a multidisciplinary team of about 50 KATH health professionals joined local health workers during the installation of a new chief and queen mother. The team conducted health education and screening exercises and engaged the public through radio programmes as part of the hospital’s contribution to the community. Dr. Larbi said other activities lined up include community outreach programmes involving health screening, health education and blood donation, as well as a public lecture focusing on the history and development of KATH. The public lecture will also feature research dissemination, allowing the hospital to showcase research conducted by its professionals and its contribution to healthcare knowledge. The anniversary programme is expected to culminate in a Thanksgiving Service and Grand Durbar, where outstanding workers will be recognised, followed by a dinner dance. Dr. Larbi said the celebrations provide an opportunity for the hospital to reflect on its history while positioning itself for the future. KATH’s contribution to healthcare KATH Chief Executive Officer, Dr. Paa Kwesi Baidoo, said the inclusion of sports in the anniversary programme was consistent with the hospital’s broader health mandate. “You know, Komfo Anokye is a health institution. We provide healthcare services. And exercise or sports goes with health,” he said. Dr. Baidoo said the hospital’s contribution over the past 70 years extended beyond treating patients to supporting medical education, research and the broader healthcare system. He disclosed that KATH attended to more than 364,000 patients in 2025, highlighting the scale of services provided by the institution. He said the hospital serves people from different backgrounds and continues to fulfil its mandate as a tertiary healthcare institution. Preparing for the next 70 years Dr. Baidoo also highlighted ongoing infrastructure projects intended to expand the hospital’s capacity and improve service delivery. These include a Cardiac Catheterization/Intervention Centre being undertaken through the Ghana Medical Trust Fund, the redevelopment of an abandoned office complex and the construction of a multi-floor pharmacy complex. He said the developments were part of efforts to ensure that KATH could provide expanded services as it looks towards the next 70 years. For Dr. Larbi, KATH’s contribution over its seven decades has centred on four key areas: advanced clinical care, undergraduate and postgraduate training, research, and support for lower-level healthcare institutions. He said the hospital’s research activities continue to inform healthcare practice, while professionals trained at KATH have gone on to serve in different parts of the world. As the anniversary celebrations continue, KATH is expected to use the remaining activities to celebrate its history, recognise the contribution of its staff and communities, and set the stage for its next chapter.

items.title: Black Stars: Godwin Attram replaces Desmond Ofei as assistant coach
items.description: The Ghana Football Association (GFA) has confirmed the appointment of former Ghana international Godwin Attram as assistant coach of the Black Stars. Attram joins the Black Stars technical team replacing Desmond Ofei, who will now concentrate fully on his role as head coach of the Black Meteors, Ghana’s U23 national team. The appointment forms part of the GFA’s technical restructuring as the Black Stars prepare for the upcoming 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers and other international assignments. Attram, a former Black Stars midfielder, brings a wealth of experience as both a player and a coach. The ex-PSV Eindhoven and Silkeborg IF playmaker previously served as Head Coach of Great Olympics and has been involved in various national youth team structures. He is highly regarded for his work in player development and his modern approach to the game. Desmond Ofei, who combined his role with the Black Stars with his duties as head coach of the Black Satellites and later the Black Meteors, will now focus exclusively on leading Ghana’s U23 side as they prepare for the next Olympic Games qualifiers.

En cette période de rentrée scolaire, la Brigade Mobile de Contrôle Économique et de la Répression des Fraudes (BMCRF) poursuit activement ses opérations sur l’ensemble du territoire. L’objectif est de garantir aux familles des fournitures scolaires de qualité, proposées au juste prix et en conformité avec la réglementation. Les équipes de la BMCRF sont mobilisées sur le terrain, visitant marchés et librairies pour s’assurer du respect des marges réglementés, de la transparence dans l’affichage, et de la conformité des produits proposés. Les Américano-Camerounais Joel Hans Embiid et les Philadelphia 76ers peuvent-ils aller plus loin en playoffs NBA cette saison ?
items.description: © Yellowbet Les Philadelphia 76ers ont atteint les demi-finales de la Conférence Est la saison dernière après avoir terminé avec un bilan de 45 victoires pour 37 défaites. Leur parcours en playoffs s’est toutefois arrêté face aux New York Knicks, qui se sont imposés 4-0. Ce résultat donne à Philadelphia un objectif clair pour cette nouvelle saison : atteindre les finales de conférence. L’effectif possède suffisamment de talent pour y parvenir, même si beaucoup dépendra de la disponibilité de Joel Embiid. Les 76ers ont remporté leur série du premier tour contre Boston 4-3 après avoir été menés 3–1. Ils ont ensuite affronté une équipe des Knicks qui a mis en évidence les faiblesses de Philadelphia. Cette élimination sans concéder le moindre match a également soulevé des questions sur la capacité des 76ers à compter sur Embiid tout au long d'une longue campagne de playoffs. Embiid élève le plafond de Philadelphia Lorsqu’il est en bonne santé, Embiid offre à Philadelphia un scoreur d’élite et un défenseur intérieur de premier plan. Le septuple All-Star a affiché des moyennes de 26,9 points, 7,7 rebonds et 3,9 passes décisives en 38 matchs de saison régulière la saison dernière. Ses absences ont constitué un problème majeur. Embiid a manqué une grande partie de la saison et a fait son retour pendant la série contre Boston après avoir subi une appendicectomie. Il a ensuite été gêné par une entorse à la cheville et des douleurs à la hanche durant la série face aux Knicks. Philadelphia a besoin d’un Embiid en meilleure santé cette saison. Sa présence modifie la manière dont les adversaires défendent les 76ers et donne à l’équipe une option fiable dans le jeu placé. Le fait de pouvoir compter sur lui pendant les playoffs pourrait avoir un impact plus important sur les ambitions de Philadelphia que n’importe quel changement individuel dans l’effectif. Maxey et le reste de l’effectif Tyrese Maxey apporte aux 76ers un autre scoreur et créateur de haut niveau. Sa progression continue devrait réduire la pression exercée sur Embiid, qui ne devrait pas avoir à créer presque toutes les possessions importantes. Le reste de l’effectif aura également son importance. Philadelphia devra pouvoir compter sur une adresse régulière à trois points, sur des minutes solides de la part du banc et sur suffisamment de profondeur défensive pour tenir le rythme d’une série en sept matchs. La série contre les Knicks a montré ce qui peut se produire lorsque ces éléments ne fonctionnent pas ensemble. Philadelphia a eu du mal à suivre, avant de finalement perdre le quatrième match de 30 points. Pour aller plus loin en playoffs, Maxey et les joueurs qui entourent Embiid devront être réguliers lorsque les défenses concentreront leur attention sur le pivot. Les 76ers ne peuvent pas se permettre de longues séquences durant lesquelles leur attaque devient trop prévisible. Philadelphia peut-elle atteindre les finales de conférence ? Les 76ers ont déjà montré qu’ils étaient capables de remporter une série de playoffs difficile. Leur victoire 4-3 contre Boston la saison dernière les a obligés à revenir d’un déficit de 3-1, leur offrant une expérience précieuse avant une nouvelle campagne de postseason. Pour les fans qui suivent les matchs en livestream ou utilisent des betting apps in Cameroon , les perspectives de Philadelphia dépendront probablement en grande partie de l’état de santé d’Embiid. Sa disponibilité pourrait influencer les attentes autour de l’équipe plus que presque tout autre facteur. Une qualification pour les finales de conférence est envisageable si Embiid reste en bonne santé, si Maxey continue de progresser et si le reste de l’effectif répond présent pendant les playoffs. La saison dernière s’est terminée en demi-finales ; la prochaine étape consiste à trouver suffisamment de régularité pour franchir ce tour. items.title: What Were My Dreams Trying to Tell Me?
items.description: Illustrations by Hélène Blanc W hen I was 20 years old, I started to sense a hole inside me. The feeling was utterly concrete, though the result of no medical condition that any of the various doctors I saw could identify. The hole felt like a viscous emptiness—a paradox, admittedly, as any real emptiness should have felt like nothing. This was a nothing, but its nothingness very much felt like something—and something that was growing. Accompanying this feeling of an expanding hole at the center of me was a sense that I was losing more and more of myself to it, like shoreline eroded by rising waters. To lose myself felt less like oblivion than instability. I observed in myself a new susceptibility to the opinions of others, and a new recklessness, as if some dark, decisive action might either quiet my doubts about my fundamental worth or end my longing once and for all. I recall one particularly dangerous, drunken night that had me well over the legal limit, both aware that I was getting into a car that could kill me and others, and also not believing that any of it mattered. The onset of my devolving well-being was strange and sudden, and seemed connected to childhood in some way I couldn’t understand. I hadn’t been a tortured child but rather placid, if introverted. My parents always said that I had been easy to keep happy. It sometimes seemed to me as if the hole I was experiencing was one where some piece of my childhood had once resided. My friends found my behavior disturbing. I was missing class in college, showing up to theater rehearsals drunk. A caring young woman I was dating could take no more of my savage, ranting mood swings and persistent despair. She broke up with me over tea at the student union and implored me to seek help. I knew she was right. Even sleep was now fraught with violent, terrifying dreams—of rocket ships out of control, conflagrations and invasions, and, yes, holes into which I would disappear. But exactly what sort of help I might need, I didn’t know. I confided my woes to a friend who’d grown up on a farm in Kentucky. He never missed Sunday Mass, and when I told him about the hole inside me, he pulled a copy of The Seven Storey Mountain from his bag and handed it to me. Thomas Merton, he said, had written about something similar . It was what had led him to leave the world and become a monk. I found deep resonance in the book’s harrowing account of Merton’s time at Cambridge and Columbia—the intense restlessness and emptiness, the disgust and torpor and despair. But Merton’s solution was theistic: a turn to God that I could only read as naive and distorting. I didn’t have any interest in God. Even the passages that approached the specificity of my own experience were charged with personification that read as anachronistic at best: The room was very quiet. It was rather dark, too. And as I lay in bed, in my weariness and pain and disgust, I felt for a moment the shadow of another visitor pass into the room. It was death, that came to stand by my bed. I kept my eyes closed, more out of apathy than anything else. But anyway, there was no need to open one’s eyes to see the visitor, to see death. Death is someone you see very clearly with eyes in the center of your heart: eyes that see not by reacting to light, but by reacting to a kind of a chill from within the marrow of your own life. I knew this experience: a central chill, a lightlessness connected to the doomed feeling of some ultimate end. But I resisted any characterization that departed from the fundamental sensation itself—of a growing hole inside me. For no reason I knew, I was convinced that remaining honest with myself about this basic fact was the only thing I could do to help myself. My parents were worried. They flew out to visit me at school and figure out what was wrong. Over a meal they prepared for me in a hotel room with a kitchen, I confided in them. There was a hole inside me that I needed to address, I said. They were understandably perplexed. My mother found me a psychiatrist, an avuncular Brit who was more interested in my sex life than my interior void, which I insisted was more real than he seemed willing to allow. But something important endured from the handful of sessions I had with him. A volume on the shelf over his left ear drew my fascination, and would soon fill weeks of my life: Freud’s The Interpretation of Dreams . That book began a process in me, what I’ve often called “curiosity” when I’ve told this story, but which is probably better described as a form of relationship. The nightly tumult of disturbing dreams persisted, and even if I couldn’t be sure whether Freud was right about how to make sense of them, simply attempting to do so seemed to help. Paying attention made it easier to remember my dreams, and to remember more of them. In one, I was carefully drawing an empty circle on a page of the Quran that my grandparents had given me as a boy, a circle through which—impossibly—I could reach and touch cool water. I awoke with the feeling that the hole inside me might be leading to something better, however unknown. Even so, it wasn’t until I mentioned that I was interested in dreams to a teacher I admired that I started to keep a detailed nightly log. This teacher had done a great deal of dream-work, and suggested that I tie a pencil to my finger to remind me, in those brief moments of stirring between sleep cycles, to write down whatever fragments were stirring in hypnagogic consciousness. So I did. What resulted was a daily haul of interior riches. The vividness of my unadulterated hopes and sorrows, the unusual expansiveness and wonder I experienced by night, lived on in the often-paradoxical images I would recall throughout the day. My study of Freud led to a similar scouring of the work of other psychoanalysts—and, later, mystics such as Emanuel Swedenborg, Ibn Arabi, and Rabbi Nachman—for clues about what kind of sense to be making of my dreams. In my final year of college, I encountered, in a late work of Carl Jung’s, the advice to treat dreams as meaningful psychic events, a technique to facilitate what Jung called their “compensatory” function—balancing the biases and limitations of one’s conscious attitudes. I took this to mean treating a dream’s images as real in their own right. Whether doing so had any such balancing effect on me, I can’t be sure. But my persistent despair seemed to be dimming; the hole inside me felt different the more I was able to gaze patiently into it for whatever was coming through. The dream-work was paying dividends, though what exactly was paying them out, I had no clue. Illustration by Hélène Blanc I know how what I’m about to share is likely to come off; it isn’t the first time I’ve spoken it aloud. I started to dream of things that hadn’t happened yet , to “see” things at night that then appeared in my life during the day. One of the earliest and most startling of these uncanny doublings took place in my first year after college. I was living and working in a small town in the Tuscan countryside, without a phone, before the internet. I dreamed that a friend I knew in Paris showed up on my doorstep with skis on his back. Two days later, I awoke to the sound of my name being called from down in the piazza, outside my front window. I opened the worn balcony doors to find the very friend I’d dreamed of; he’d gotten my Italian address from a mutual friend and seen that the town I was living in wasn’t too far out of the way as he made the trip from Rome up to the city in the Alps where he planned to spend a few days skiing. I resisted speaking of what had happened, lest I be impelled to name whatever in me had seized my bewildered attention. The Tuscan episode was not the last time dream and day seemed to cross wires. Years later, I would dream of a terrorist attack on Manhattan two days before 9/11, and of a malign, cough-inducing fog slowly engulfing the world several weeks before the eruption of the coronavirus into my (and the world’s) awareness—improbable coincidences I struggled to accept as such. And yet, these visions became the occasion to doubt any picture of the universe that failed to make room for what could only be experienced as a kind of magic. If the prognosticating mode had been the only benefit to accrue from my attention to my dreams, I might not have been so diligent in my recordkeeping. After all, I wasn’t seeing stock prices or lottery numbers, the only rationale many might have accepted for my habit of destroying every good night’s rest. For at that point, I was waking up every 45 minutes to reach for the bedside pad on which I made notes about whatever was moving around inside me. But my night work was opening up creative vistas. One mentor, well-versed in working with the unconscious, suggested that it was enlarging the space of what she kept calling—despite my confusion about what she really meant by it—my psyche. [ Read: McNeal, a play by Ayad Akhtar ] Indeed, a growing spaciousness was now my sense of the interior core where the hole had opened up. The hole itself wasn’t gone, but it had changed character, less a wound now than an opening, though I couldn’t always tell the difference. And yet, the trajectory seemed to be shifting. That pliant, receptive brightness bearing the imprint of something more than just my name, the self, began to feel heightened, enlarged. I had learned that some cultures conceived of the self as containing two parts: a smaller, individual, daily self, and a larger, multiple, primordial one. This greater self, it was believed, was the one that dreamed. Something about this way of thinking felt more useful—and more reflective of my experience—than any of the latest studies in neuroscience I read about the physiological functions of dreams. Psyche : Greek for “soul.” Which felt like a more appropriate frame of reference—despite my continued resistance to the language of theism—for experiences that so evidently defied the materialist doctrines of my late-20th-century education. To privilege the Newtonian model of classical mechanics—one object pushing or pulling another, all the way down to the molecules that formed consciousness—over the actual data of my experience felt like intellectual laziness. I understood that others would see my willingness to abide more patiently in the mystery as irrational. My usage of the Greek term started to give way to its English corollary. The word soul seemed to make better sense of whatever was expanding inside me, a rising that was also a deepening, married to the uncanny knowing of what seemed like prognostication, and, more valuably, to a natural empathy for others. And in case this comes off as more altruistic than seems reasonable: Less blinded by myself, more porous to others, I found, too, that I was becoming a better writer. [ From the November 2024 issue: Jeffrey Goldberg, Ayad Akhtar, Robert Downey Jr., and Bartlett Sher on writing in the age of AI ] Soul was, for me then, a mode of being mostly experienced in images by night that shaped my understanding by day—for example, that a close friend was like the abandoned dog I dreamed he was, long neglected by his family, never allowed into the house; an image that helped me navigate his touchiness, providing readier access to the wellspring of loving loyalty that coursed beneath his habitual choler. I found in the use of soul a capaciousness that not only accounted for this richer relationship to others and the world—and to myself—but served as a bridge to deeper mystery, and to a new patience that allowed me to acclimate to it. There were other benefits, too. Just as the vital, vivid stuff of my brain’s nightlife enriched my being—to use a word that joined soul in the lexicon of descriptive terms of dubious provenance—so did my immersion in dream dross seem to feed my capacities with language. There was a stronger tether now between word and thing, a tether, paradoxically, that operated simultaneously in many directions and layers. The webbed, protean mode of associative thinking—one thing reaching for another, in opposing vectors at once—was less an effort than a reflex, more instinctive than the ordinal fixity of my usual habits of mind. Shakespeare, whom I’d long struggled to apprehend, now made easier sense, even as the experience of reading him felt like perpetual entry into undiscovered country, the phonetic expatiations, the dense semantic clusters, the sounds and images opening up more and more effortlessly into a particular state of absorptive flow, a pleasing emotional and intellectual static that I took to calling “linguistic space.” I started taking a yoga class on the Upper West Side. Our becalming teacher spent the better part of our weekly hour teaching us to meditate. Setting aside my irritation with her hushed and holy tones, I found myself growing more susceptible to her instructions. I could catch a gap between thoughts that felt curiously similar to a rich blankness that resulted from hours spent in linguistic space. The fixed point of focus on the breath sharpened my mind and filled it with something closer to light than thought. On my own, I began to sit—sometimes for hours—in this pregnant blankness, exhibiting a facility for what the yoga teacher called “practice” that I couldn’t explain. My weekly hour with that yoga teacher sparked an interest in meditation that led to weeks, and years, of working with other instructors of inner techniques. I learned to visualize and hold in memory shapes derived from Gnostic practices and colors derived from Sufi ones. Intoning Abulafia’s list of Hebrew names for God at the proper pitch and volume shook the bones in my ear and nerves along my neck. Calm was promised, and often followed, though I wondered whether this said more about my susceptibility to suggestion than the practices themselves. Sometimes what followed was stranger. Once, as I sat in a darkened room at dusk, observing the breath going in and out of me, I felt that breath begin to breathe itself. In the half shadows, with my eyes closed, a startling brightness waxed and waned with the movement of air. What was this light? I wondered. Was this just the room’s faint light filtering through my eyelids, brightening and dimming as my pupils dilated and contracted with each breath? If so, was this suggestion too? I would come to no definitive answer. The inner light continued to strobe. If it was all suggestion, I didn’t mind. It was getting me further than faith had. From Meister Eckhart I learned to recognize in my meditative blankness a silence clean of longing, one that, if I could remain in it, would release an astonishing vitality. Others I studied with found it strange that my interest in meditation would be piqued by dream-work and quickened by pentameter. They sometimes remarked that what I was up to resembled anthropology more than devotion. They were only partly right. To me, it was all a study in being, or soul, or spirit (the latest addition to my lexicon)—which is to say, an inquiry into the substance and nature of the interior life. My reading, too, reflected the scavenging of a magpie in search of material from which to build its nest: the Phaedrus and Patanjali and Mulla Sadra; Being and Time one month, Mathnawi the next. What exactly I thought I was doing was not a matter of concern as long as I kept to myself about it. What I’m compressing into paragraphs here took so much longer, of course, and was hardly as sequential as telling makes it sound. I kept at it for the reward of the work itself. I had experiences of rapture (and sorrow) so deep, of pleasures so unprecedented, it was sometimes hard to return to the dishes and the rent. But I had studied with a remarkable Vedic teacher who warned me about seeking states rather than the truth. “What is the truth?” I once asked him as we sauntered along a Tennessee creek. He pulled his orange robe tighter against a rising spring wind. He was too smart to oblige. “The truth is not like knowledge about that tree,” he said, pointing to a blooming magnolia. “Only the tree knows its truth.” I didn’t want to pretend I understood him. “You write stories,” he said. “Inside the story is a meaning that is the reason for it. Not words that carry it, but the wordless substance of its truth you take away.” Despite my customary reticence about such things, I had occasions to compare notes with fellow travelers. One evening, at a fundraising function downtown, I found myself sharing martinis with a physician whose lived-in eloquence about his Zen practice felt like an opening. I was not expecting the lesson in brain science he proceeded to impart: I’d become addicted, he said, to activating certain parts of my cerebral cortex. Like an addict—I flinched at that word—I was pulling on neurological switches, training my brain to release its own pleasure chemicals through a growing grab bag of inner tricks. Clearly he didn’t approve. I was too embarrassed to ask why, even as I recalled my teacher’s warning not to chase states, but rather to seek the wordless substance of truth. I resisted the physician’s account even as I couldn’t ignore the unease it stirred in me. Illustration by Hélène Blanc M y fellow traveler was right, at least as far as neuroscience went. Studies were beginning to show that meditation—a loose term for the various practices of inner focus I was involved with—activated and deactivated specific parts of the human brain. In the 1990s, the neuroscientist Andrew Newberg studied advanced Tibetan monks and Franciscan nuns as they entered deep meditative states . The results were strikingly similar. In both groups, areas of the brain believed to be responsible for orienting us in space and time showed markedly decreased activity, as if the neural basis for the boundary between self and other had gone quiet. They were using very different techniques, but the results, neurologically speaking, were nearly indistinguishable. Each group, however, described the experience differently: the nuns as a feeling of union with Christ, the monks as a state of emptiness. I knew enough about Buddhism to recognize in that word, emptiness , something very different from the hole that had opened up inside me during early adulthood. For the Buddhist, perception of the nature of reality discloses the identity of emptiness with form, and form with emptiness. It’s a perception described in other traditions by other means, and sometimes, in Christianity, as an annihilation of the individual personality in the presence of God. The maps and words and techniques were different; somehow, the underlying experience itself, beyond words or ideas, was the same. Not quite in the words of my Vedic teacher: The brain scans were a story containing a truth known only to the one inside them. F or a long time , all of this felt like little more than a motley, life-enhancing assortment, which is not to downplay the valuable place it had in my life. Rightly or wrongly, I attributed the return of my fundamental stability after the harrowing years of early adulthood—and the return of the placid, placable self I’d known much earlier in life—to my commitment to daily practice. I would come to think of inner work as an adult corollary to the joyous absorption of childhood play. I’d found a way to play again, I concluded, and somehow this had seemed to “fill” the hole again. But the life of the spirit was not what I took my real life to be. I was a writer. I wanted to know the broken world that was, not the healed one that could be. I had no fundamental interest in escaping the human condition. To the extent that spirit—or soulfulness—anchored my curiosity, quickened my perceptions, deepened my empathy, I rationalized its creative and analytical utility. In truth, something less tangible than optimization bound me to practice. It kept me in the company of more eternal conundrums, questions of consciousness and origin and meaning for which, of course, I expected no answer. But proximity to the unknown—living contact with it, if you will—seemed like a worthy form of knowledge. In this, I was like many friends who took psychedelics; I wanted to recover the awe and mystery I recognized in their accounts when they shared them. For the most part, though, I was still doing what my teacher had warned me against—chasing states. In part, this was a function of resisting meaning. I had been too respectful of my teacher back then to tell him I wasn’t sure that a story’s meaning mattered to me the way he assumed it would. But I felt the slow accretion of a wordless substance inside me, not well-being or certainty or the rapture of some fugitive sublime, but something I might call intimacy: intimacy with an inwardness spied only indirectly, whose purer acquaintance I seemed to be making very slowly indeed. With the hindsight of decades, I can track a tectonic shift away from the visible to something more diffuse and sustaining, an interior through line that has both warned me against the tyranny of acquisition—of things, of states—and provided the means of finding sustenance in absence. Whatever this is, whatever name I might give it, I can’t deny that it all seems to have proceeded from that perception of a hole I felt or imagined when I was younger. William James might have called it a “sick soul”; I still don’t feel entirely confident about what word to use for the continuity that I’ve found or constructed, though some word has always been necessary. I had spent years resisting every vocabulary that exceeded the raw data of sensation, only to find that this austerity, too, had to be exceeded. Too much of what mattered most in my own life had remained unspoken not because it was unreal, but because I did not know how to bring it into language without betraying it. For decades, I steered conversations away from these inner experiences, obedient to the rule that such things could not be talked about without sounding foolish or deranged. But my reticence began to feel like capitulation to falseness. It took me years to understand that my silence was not only protective but deforming—for without others to hear it, the still, small voice within was so much harder to discern. And yet, the silence was not my own to break. With so little room in our common life for such things, we have no common language for them either. Ralph Waldo Emerson knew the problem. In “ The Over-Soul ,” he wrote that language could not paint this “subtile” order of our experience in its own colors; but he knew how important it was to keep trying. The great Russian novelists knew it too, treating soul not as a word reserved for Sundays, but as the moral substance of life. I’ve found myself mourning not their metaphysics but their seriousness, their acceptance of the inscrutable boundlessness of the inner life—unruly, morally consequent—as a subject for public speech. What matters to me now is less the defense of any particular term than the search for a language in which such things can be spoken of seriously, in fiction and elsewhere, without piety or diagnosis. Without a language for speaking openly together about the inner life, what often matters most to us remains locked away, inaccessible to the inquiry and challenge vital to all knowledge. As I finished a draft of this essay, I had a dream. In it, I stood at the edge of a well—another hole, I realized as I made note the following morning—where there was no bucket to draw water. Around it moved countless people in a flurried hubbub, shepherds and masons and architects, all of us trying to figure out how to draw the water whose surface we could see in the faint shimmering at the bottom. It was going to take time, I thought, before we figured it out—just as I awoke. This article appears in the November 2026 print edition with the headline “In My Dreams.” When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

items.title: In Defense of Guilt by Association
items.description: J. D. Vance and Abdul El-Sayed have very little in common ideologically and seem to like each other even less. As part of a nasty exchange of personal insults last month, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan implied that Vance’s grandfather would disapprove of the vice president’s Indian American wife. In response , Vance called El-Sayed “very, very evil” and warned him to “keep my wife’s name the hell out of your mouth because she’s way out of your league.” Yet even as Vance and El-Sayed are happy to trade schoolyard taunts, they can agree on at least one thing: that guilt by association is a contemptible means of scoring cheap political points. “I’m tired of this guilt-by-association thing,” El-Sayed complained earlier this year, when he was asked about his decision to campaign alongside Hasan Piker, an internet shock jock who has said that “America deserved 9/11,” described allegations of sexual violence on October 7 as “rape fantasies,” and praised Mao Zedong as “one of the great leaders of the world,” among many other charming bon mots. Despite repeated calls from within his own party to renounce Piker, El-Sayed refuses to do so. Vance is facing a similar situation with his friend Tucker Carlson. Vance “ doesn’t believe in guilt-by-association cancel culture ,” a spokesperson said in September 2024, after the then-senator appeared onstage with the conservative podcast host. In the years since his firing from Fox News, Carlson has lauded a Holocaust denier as “the most important historian in the United States,” accused a small Jewish sect of orchestrating the war in Iran, and praised Vladimir Putin as “the most effective leader in my lifetime.” Carlson, whose show returns again and again to the supposed perfidy of the Jews, has become the country’s highest-profile promoter of anti-Semitism. He recently held a friendly conversation with a guest who claimed that algebra was “fake math” created for “goy slaves.” Vance was asked directly about his relationship with Carlson at a White House press conference earlier this month. “Tucker is a friend, despite the fact that we disagree on a number of things,” the vice president said. “And I’m not going to play the game where I throw friends under the bus because I have political disagreements with them. I think that is a terrible place for the United States to go.” [ Jonathan Chait: J. D. Vance’s disingenuous defense of Tucker Carlson ] El-Sayed and Vance would have us believe that their troublesome friends are no different from the people in our own lives whose political views we abhor but whom we nonetheless love and appreciate. “If I had to choose between betraying my country and betraying my friend, I hope I should have the guts to betray my country,” the English writer E. M. Forster wrote in 1938 as Europe hurtled toward war. It’s a noble sentiment, a paean to friendship over tribe. But Piker and Carlson are not the equivalent of your crazy uncle. And El-Sayed and Vance are not regular citizens; they’re political figures whose judgment and choices affect other Americans’ lives. One’s choice of friends is in fact an excellent sign of character, and in this respect, both Vance and El-Sayed have demonstrated a conspicuous lack of it. The tactic known as “guilt by association” evokes the legacy of Senator Joe McCarthy, whose feral zeal for exposing Communists, real or imagined, was so era-defining that it inspired the attachment of an ism to his surname. McCarthy’s sin wasn’t his anti-communism, however—there were indeed highly placed Soviet agents in the federal government. It was his recklessness and lack of concern for the truth. There has to be a reasonable middle ground between conducting a witch hunt and blatantly ignoring someone’s willingness to fraternize with genuinely disreputable people. Now that their associations are in the spotlight, El-Sayed, Vance, and their respective ideological compatriots are eager to minimize them. In a softball interview with Piker several months ago, the Pod Save Americ a host Jon Favreau, a prominent liberal opinion-shaper, said that he wants Democrats to take the “Don’t Talk About Hasan Piker For A Day Challenge.” Asked about Piker’s remarks concerning 9/11, El-Sayed tried to depict himself as a victim of the “cancel culture that all of us agreed was a bad idea back in 2020, but we seem to want to bring back.” A “Vance ally” echoed a similar sentiment to The Washington Post about the vice president’s relationship with Carlson, saying , “We’re done with the canceling, period.” No one should accept these evasions. In April, El-Sayed deployed Piker to boost support among young voters at Michigan State and the University of Michigan. In the final hours before polls closed, El-Sayed appeared at a pool party with Piker and other internet influencers in Detroit. Vance’s association with Carlson goes much deeper. In a 2021 interview recalling the time they first met, Vance described their immediate recognition of each other as “the guy who’s exactly right about what’s going on in the country.” Carlson helped persuade Donald Trump to select Vance as his running mate; Vance hired Carlson’s son as his deputy press secretary. When Vance guest-hosted Charlie Kirk’s show after the conservative activist’s assassination, one of the first people he invited into the vice-presidential suite was Carlson. (At Kirk’s funeral six days later, Carlson delivered a eulogy that seemed to imply that the Jews had murdered Kirk just as they had Jesus Christ.) The most obvious reason El-Sayed and Vance haven’t disowned their noxious friends is that both Piker and Carlson command large audiences. Politics is about winning votes, and a moral miscreant’s is worth the same as a saint’s. Other politicians have done much worse than associate with the likes of Piker and Carlson. What’s more troubling is that El-Sayed and Vance both appear to sympathize with at least some of what their influencer friend espouses. On multiple occasions, Vance has shown that he either doesn’t understand or doesn’t care about anti-Semitism. He once dismissed outrage over a group of Young Republicans joking about gas chambers as “pearl clutching” and characterized attempts to sideline bigots from the conservative movement as “endless, self-defeating purity tests.” One might think that Carlson’s frequent attacks on Vance’s boss, up to and including that Trump “ should be removed from office immediately ,” would have persuaded Vance, purely out of his own self-interest, to disavow Carlson. That he hasn’t done so indicates the high value he places on his association with him. If not for such data points, Vance’s friendship with Carlson would be easy to dismiss as misplaced affection for someone who helped advance his career. But Vance is on the record stating otherwise. Late last year, he said, I find the idea that Tucker Carlson—who has one of the largest podcasts in the world, who has millions of listeners, who supported Donald Trump in the 2024 election, who supported me in the 2024 election—the idea that his views are somehow completely anathema to conservatism, that he has no place in the conservative movement, is frankly absurd. This implies that Holocaust denial, claims of Jewish disloyalty to the United States, veneration of Putin, and a host of other poisonous ideas are welcome in the conservative movement. Even the white-nationalist influencer Nick Fuentes is fed up with Vance’s disingenuousness. “JD Vance panders to the far right but simply doesn’t want the baggage of associating with the far right,” Fuentes told The New York Times . “If he has a problem with ‘antisemites,’ then he should start by disavowing his best friend Tucker Carlson.” [ Read: The Hasan Piker question ] A similar ideological affinity appears to exist between Piker and El-Sayed, whose past statements on 9/11 and terrorism more broadly have a way of creating a moral equivalency between the United States and its Islamist enemies. “Today, I mourn the 3K lives, 6K injuries, & infrastructural devastation in NYC, perpetuated ignorantly in the name of my faith,” El-Sayed tweeted five years ago on the 20th anniversary of the attacks. “Tomorrow, I’ll mourn ~1M lives, millions of injuries, & infrastructural devastation in 3 countries, perpetuated ignorantly in the name of my country.” Earlier this year, after a Hezbollah-inspired terrorist rammed his car into a Detroit-area synagogue where 140 preschool-age Jewish children were playing, El-Sayed said that “hurt people hurt people,” a reference to the fact that the attacker had lost four relatives in an Israeli air strike. (In a clumsy attempt at an apology, El-Sayed stubbornly refused to acknowledge the odious logic of his remarks, allowing only that he had chosen to administer “the right medicine at the wrong time.”) Like Prince Hal banishing Falstaff from the royal court , sometimes ending a friendship is a sign of the maturity necessary to lead. Barack Obama made just such a choice in 2008 after the hateful and conspiratorial remarks of his longtime pastor, Jeremiah Wright, were exposed to the world. Obama’s relationship with Wright was much more intimate than that between El-Sayed and Piker or Vance and Carlson; he had sat in Wright’s pews for decades, and Wright had baptized his children. And yet Obama ultimately turned his back on Wright, saying that the preacher’s divisive, anti-American “rants” were “an insult to what we’ve been trying to do in this campaign.” Obama understood that as long as he was associated with a character like Wright, he could never be a credible advocate for the national unity he claimed to seek. J. D. Vance and Abdul El-Sayed each face a much easier decision—and each has failed to make the right one. It’s a testament to Americans’ increasing tolerance for extremism that both men seem to be getting away with it.

items.description: a Macina, le prix du mil connaît une forte hausse sur les marches. Depuis le samedi 19 septembre 2026, le sac de 50 kilos se vend entre 30 000 et 32 500 francs CFA, contre 19 000 a 20 000 francs il y a quelques jours. Selon les commercants, cette flambee s'explique notamment par la rarete du mil, liee a l'insuffisance des pluies dans le cercle. items.title: Iboga : quand l’argent menace de dénaturer la spiritualité
items.description: Face à la montée du tourisme spirituel autour de l’iboga et du Bwété, Guy Bertrand Mapangou, président du Conseil économique, social, environnemental et culturel (CESEC), alerte sur la marchandisation des savoirs initiatiques. Pour lui, la vente de titres de « Nimas » et de connaissances traditionnelles à des étrangers constitue une menace culturelle et spirituelle qui pourrait finir par vider le Bwété de son sens. Pour Guy Bertrand Mapangou, président du CESEC, vendre l'iboga et ses savoirs associés est un danger culturel et spirituel. © GabonReview / Illustration IA Depuis une dizaine d’années, l’iboga, et notamment l’ibogaïne qui en est issue, bénéficie d’une réputation internationale grandissante en raison de son potentiel étudié dans le traitement des addictions et des traumatismes. Cette notoriété croissante attire toutefois des réseaux et des individus intéressés par sa dimension spirituelle et thérapeutique, ouvrant la voie à une véritable économie autour des pratiques initiatiques gabonaises. Dans une tribune particulièrement critique, Guy Bertrand Mapangou dénonce l’existence de réseaux organisés de trafiquants opérant au Gabon et à l’étranger, avec, selon lui, la complicité de certains Gabonais, tradipraticiens, initiés et même dépositaires de la tradition. Il leur reproche notamment de monnayer auprès d’étrangers des titres de Nimas et des savoirs issus de l’initiation. «Vendre l’iboga et ses savoirs associés est un danger culturel et spirituel », affirme-t-il, estimant qu’un savoir initiatique ne saurait être réduit à une marchandise. « Un savoir initiatique ne se vend pas. Un rite se vit, il ne se consomme pas comme un forfait bien-être », martèle le président du CESEC. Pour Mapangou, la transformation de l’initiation en produit touristique accessible à ceux qui peuvent payer constitue une rupture avec les fondements du Bwété. Il pointe particulièrement la responsabilité des gardiens de la tradition qui accepteraient de vendre des titres ou des connaissances sans respecter le parcours spirituel qu’ils supposent. « Ce n’est plus du Bwété, c’est du folklore commercial », tranche-t-il, évoquant également l’exposition des auteurs à des sanctions pénales. Guy Bertrand Mapangou voit dans ce processus une menace plus profonde Au-delà de la question financière, l’ancien ministre voit dans cette marchandisation une menace plus profonde : celle d’un bouleversement des critères de légitimité spirituelle. « Cette situation ouvre une brèche que rien ne peut refermer facilement : celle où l’argent devient le nouveau critère de légitimité spirituelle, à la place du respect, de la transmission et du sens », prévient-il. L’alerte porte ainsi sur la préservation d’un patrimoine spirituel que le président du CESEC considère comme intimement lié à l’identité culturelle gabonaise. « L’iboga a survécu à la colonisation, aux interdits, à l’oubli. Il ne survivra pas nécessairement à l’indifférence des initiés qui devraient le protéger en premier », écrit-il. Pour Guy Bertrand Mapangou, l’enjeu dépasse donc la seule protection d’une plante. L’iboga, ou «Éboghè», demeure à ses yeux un élément central du Bwété, à la fois support de guérison, de révélation et de transmission. Mais sa valeur spirituelle se trouve aujourd’hui confrontée aux logiques commerciales nées de sa notoriété internationale. « L’iboga est bien un pont vivant entre les vivants et les ancêtres, le cœur battant du rite Bwété », rappelle-t-il, avant de résumer son inquiétude : « Éboghè sert à guérir, à révéler, à transmettre. Aujourd’hui il sert aussi à s’enrichir. Et c’est là que le problème commence ». L’article Iboga : quand l’argent menace de dénaturer la spiritualité est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .
